sections.h: 3 Maccabees: a king barred from the sanctuary
sections.b: In 3 Maccabees, Ptolemy IV of Egypt, fresh from his victory at Raphia (217 BC), sacrifices at the temple in Jerusalem and then demands to enter the sanctuary. The priests read him the law: no Gentile may enter, and only the high priest, once a year (3 Maccabees 1:11). The whole city prays, the high priest Simon reminds God that he chose this place for his name although his own dwelling is "the heaven of heaven" (3 Maccabees 2:15-16), and God strikes the king down. The story follows the pattern of Heliodorus in 2 Maccabees 3; C. W. Emmet (1913) saw no direct borrowing between the two books, only a shared school and period. Both stand in a line with Uzziah, struck in the temple (2 Chronicles 26:16-20).

The rule of Leviticus 16, that only the high priest may go behind the veil, and only on the Day of Atonement, is the law the priests read to Ptolemy IV in 3 Maccabees 1:11-12. Hebrews 9:7 states the same rule, and so, later, does the Mishnah (Kelim 1:9).

3 Maccabees gives the high priest Simon, whom C. W. Emmet (1913) takes to be Simon II, perhaps the Simon whom Sirach praises (Sirach 50:1-21), a long prayer when Ptolemy IV threatens the sanctuary (3 Maccabees 2:1-20). The priests first answer the king with the law and then lie face down in their robes (3 Maccabees 1:11-16), a picture very close to 2 Maccabees 3:15.

3 Maccabees names the high priest of Ptolemy IV's day as Simon (2:1), and C. W. Emmet (1913) identifies him with Simon II, son of Onias II, perhaps the Simon praised in Sirach 50. In the story his prayer moves God to strike down the king who tried to enter the sanctuary (3 Maccabees 2:1-22). Jewish tradition also remembers a high priest Simon, Simon the Righteous, who met Alexander the Great in his robes and saved the temple (Bavli Yoma 69a).

In 3 Maccabees 1 some young men in Jerusalem call for arms, but the elders turn them back to prayer (1:23), and it is the high priest Simon's prayer that saves the temple (2:1-21). The prayer recalls God's past judgments on the proud, the Flood, Sodom and Pharaoh, and Solomon's promise that God would hear prayer made in this house (1 Kings 8:33-34; 2 Chronicles 20:9). It ends with words from the Greek of Psalm 79:8.

sections.h: The Jews of Egypt under Ptolemy IV
sections.b: 3 Maccabees is set among the Jews of Ptolemaic Egypt in the reign of Ptolemy IV Philopator (died 204 BC): in Alexandria and in the countryside (the chōra) along the Nile. It opens with his victory over Antiochus III at Raphia in 217 BC, which Polybius also describes (Histories 5.79-86), and C. W. Emmet (1913) takes Daniel 11:11-12 to refer to it.

sections.h: Citizenship at the price of the law
sections.b: In 3 Maccabees the king offers the Jews of Alexandria equal citizenship with the Greek citizens of the city, if they join the mysteries of Dionysus (3 Maccabees 2:30). A few accept; most refuse and shun those who went over (2:31-33). The story turns a real hope of Alexandrian Jews, civic equality, into a test of faithfulness.

Dionysus was the family god of the Ptolemies, and a later Greek dictionary says Ptolemy IV was tattooed with ivy leaves (both reported by C. W. Emmet, 1913). In 3 Maccabees he orders that registered Jews be branded with the ivy leaf, the god's emblem (3 Maccabees 2:29), and offers citizenship to those initiated in his mysteries (2:30). 2 Maccabees 6:7 tells of Jews forced to march in Dionysus's parade carrying ivy under Antiochus IV.

3 Maccabees tells of a king who ordered Jews "to have the mark of Dionysus, an ivy leaf, burned into his body" (3 Maccabees 2:29). The verb, charassō, is from the same root as Revelation's charagma. In both books a ruler's cult demands a mark on the body, and the faithful refuse. The law forbade such marks (Leviticus 19:28).

In 3 Maccabees 2:28 the king orders all the Jews of Alexandria to be put on the census rolls (the laographia, a list of people for taxes) and lowered to the status of slaves. C. W. Emmet (1913) reports that the word is found in Ptolemaic papyri for a tax list of people who were mostly native Egyptians; Victor Tcherikover (1945) linked the verse with the census under Augustus that listed those who paid the poll tax.

The high priest's prayer in 3 Maccabees 2:4 names the giants among those God destroyed with "water without measure," following the Greek of Genesis 6:4 (gigantes). Sirach 16:7 and Wisdom 14:6 make the same link between the giants and divine judgment.
Simon's prayer names Sodom's sin as arrogance and says God made the city a warning to later generations (3 Maccabees 2:5), as Ezekiel 16:49 names its pride and 2 Peter 2:6 calls it an example.
3 Maccabees 2:6-8 retells the plagues and the drowning of Pharaoh's chariots, and the praise of those carried across, as a model for God's judgment on a proud king of Egypt.

Simon's prayer says that God, who needs nothing, chose Jerusalem and made the place holy for his name (3 Maccabees 2:9), and that he promised to hear prayer there (2:10). It is built on Deuteronomy 12:5 and Solomon's prayer (1 Kings 8:29-30).

3 Maccabees names the food laws as the reason some neighbors hated the Jews of Egypt: "they kept themselves apart in the matter of food" (3 Maccabees 3:4). The writer defends them: they were loyal and did what was right (3:3-5). Haman's charge in Esther 3:8 and Daniel's refusal of the king's food (Daniel 1:8) are its biblical background.

sections.h: Friendly and hostile Gentiles in 3 Maccabees
sections.b: 3 Maccabees separates the hostile "foreigners" who slandered the Jews (3:6-7) from "the Greeks in the city," who knew they had done no wrong, comforted them, and in some cases secretly promised to shield them (3:8-10). The king's own officers even join the Jews in prayer at the temple (1:27).

The letter of Ptolemy IV in 3 Maccabees 3:12-29 follows the pattern of the Persian king's letter in the Greek Esther (Addition B, at Esther 3:13): one people with strange laws, disloyal, to be destroyed with wives and children. In both books a second letter reverses the first (3 Maccabees 7:1-9; Esther's Addition E).
